digest.top_line: LS-SCLC phase 3: 54 Gy/30 fx BID SIB vs 45 Gy BID, mOS 60.7 vs 39.5 mo, HR 0.55 (0.37–0.72), p=0.003; similar toxicity, DSMB stopped at interim.
digest.tldr: Thoracic led: 54 Gy BID SIB improved OS (HR 0.55) and local PFS (HR 0.51) in LS-SCLC without added G3–4 oesophagitis or pneumonitis, stopped at interim. In breast, exploratory pooled data show tamoxifen cut 15-yr IBR to 11.4% vs 19.0% in unirradiated good-risk DCIS; retrospective proton PMRT capsular contracture HR 1.76 lost significance on MVA (P=.083).

sites.intro: Two questions next to the RT decision, both from non-randomised comparisons: tamoxifen as the lever when good-risk DCIS skips RT, and whether PBS proton PMRT adds implant capsular contracture over IMRT.

studies.name: Pencil beam scanning proton vs IMRT photon PMRT: capsular contracture risk
studies.tldr: Proton vs photon PMRT CC HR 1.76 (0.93-3.32, P=.083) on MVA; 2-yr CC 50% with protons plus DTI.
details: 🔍 Retrospective IRB-approved cohort, 2 centers within a single institution, Jan 2017 to Dec 2023
🔍 N=175: 89 PBS proton, 86 IMRT photon PMRT
🔍 Subpectoral 2-stage TE/I or DTI reconstruction; TE irradiated in all TE/I pts
🔍 Median age 49 (range 24-78); 63% Hispanic
⚠️ Cohorts imbalanced on reconstruction type (TE/I vs DTI, P<.001) and laterality (P<.001)

details.text: 📊 2-yr CC rate by modality and reconstruction type (overall P<.001)

details: 📐 Median f/u 42 mo proton vs 47 mo photon
📐 CC by Kaplan-Meier; Cox results checked with binary logistic regression
⚠️ PMRT dose, fractionation and superficial dose constraints not reported in source abstract
⚠️ Photon DTI stratum only n=15; that 2-yr estimate is imprecise
⚠️ CC definition and grading scale not stated in source abstract

verdict.rationale: Retrospective cohort with reconstruction type imbalanced between modalities (P<.001); proton effect lost significance on multivariable analysis, so the modality signal stays confounded.
verdict.audience: Subpectoral implant reconstruction (TE/I or DTI) receiving PMRT

studies.significance: The proton excess persists within both reconstruction types (2-yr CC 23% vs 12% after TE/I, 50% vs 35% after DTI) even though the adjusted HR crossed 1. Dose, fractionation and superficial constraints are not reported in source, so the PBS planning lever behind it is unknown. It bears on proton selection for implant pts.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt planned for subpectoral DTI reconstruction who is being considered for PBS proton PMRT, this questions that pairing (2-yr CC 50%); it does not address autologous or prepectoral reconstruction.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective**, IRB-approved cohort from 2 centers within a single institution, Jan 2017 to Dec 2023. Hypothesis stated a priori: **proton cohort would have higher CC**. Median follow-up 42 mo proton, 47 mo photon.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Subpectoral 2-stage TE/I or DTI** reconstruction with PMRT; N=175 (89 proton, 86 photon). Median age 49 (range 24-78), 63% Hispanic. Groups balanced except **laterality and reconstruction type (both P<.001)**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Pencil beam scanning proton vs IMRT photon** PMRT; the TE was irradiated in all TE/I pts. Dose, fractionation, bolus and superficial dose constraints are **not reported in source**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Capsular contracture** by Kaplan-Meier; associated factors by Cox proportional hazards, verified with binary logistic regression.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Reconstruction type was the only factor that stayed associated on multivariable analysis; the proton effect **did not reach significance** after adjustment (see tables).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source frames proton vs photon CC data as scarce and reports this as the **largest PBS PMRT reconstruction cohort** to date. RADCOMP compares proton vs photon breast RT on cardiac outcomes, not reconstruction complications, so it will not settle this question.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents subpectoral TE/I or DTI implant reconstruction receiving PBS proton or IMRT photon PMRT. Does not represent autologous or prepectoral reconstruction.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Photon DTI stratum is only n=15, so the within-DTI modality contrast is underpowered. CC grading scale and RT planning parameters are absent from the abstract, which blocks translation to a specific planning change.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Adjusted proton HR 1.76 with an interval of **0.93-3.32** excludes neither no effect nor a large one; P=.083 is not reassurance. The consistent direction within both reconstruction types is the stronger signal, and **PBS plus DTI** is where the risk concentrates.

studies.interpretation:
The takeaway most readers will carry, that protons raise capsular contracture risk, is weaker than the abstract's conclusion suggests. The univariate proton HR of 2.3 (1.26-4.30) falls to 1.76 (0.93-3.32) once covariates enter the model, and the only factor that kept a strong association was direct-to-implant reconstruction, HR 3.0 (1.7-5.5). That attenuation is the central methodological fact. Reconstruction type was unevenly distributed between cohorts (P<.001): 36 of the 89 proton pts had DTI against 15 of the 86 photon pts. An unadjusted modality comparison is therefore partly a comparison of reconstruction strategies.

The confidence interval tells a reader how to hold the adjusted result. An interval running from 0.93 to 3.32 rules out neither no effect nor a clinically large one, and with only 15 photon DTI pts the study cannot separate a modality effect within DTI from noise. Reading P=.083 as evidence that protons are safe with implants would be as wrong as reading the univariate HR as proof of harm. The stratified 2-yr rates are more persuasive than either model: the proton rate is higher within DTI (50% vs 35%) and within TE/I (23% vs 12%). Those are still unadjusted Kaplan-Meier estimates, and the overall P<.001 cannot by itself apportion the spread between modality and reconstruction type.

The abstract does not say why a proton excess would exist, and that limits what a radiation oncologist can do with it. A plausible mechanism would involve how PBS handles superficial dose around the implant and chest wall, but the source reports no dose, fractionation, bolus, skin constraint or planning technique. Without those, the finding cannot become a planning change, and a center with different superficial dose handling may or may not reproduce it. The laterality imbalance (P<.001) adds another layer. It plausibly reflects which pts were referred for protons, and referral patterns can carry confounders the model did not capture.

The source frames the case for proton PMRT around better cardiac and pulmonary dosimetry, and RADCOMP is testing that case on cardiac outcomes. This cohort offers a counterweight specific to implant reconstruction. It does not argue against protons in general. It argues that the reconstruction plan belongs in the modality decision, and that PBS combined with DTI is where the signal concentrates. Median follow-up of 42 and 47 months is not the weak point; confounding is. The finding would be wrong if the proton excess reflects referral pattern, surgical practice or era rather than dose. A cohort matched or stratified on reconstruction type, with superficial dose metrics reported, is what would settle it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The proton excess lost significance on MVA (HR 1.76, 0.93-3.32), but 2-yr CC stayed higher with protons after both TE/I (23% vs 12%) and DTI (50% vs 35%). Dose, fractionation and superficial constraints are not reported, so the planning lever is unknown. It bears on proton selection for implant pts.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Reconstruction type carried the strongest association: DTI vs TE/I HR 3.0 (1.7-5.5), P<.001, with the TE irradiated in all TE/I pts. For a pt expected to need PMRT, this bears on DTI vs 2-stage planning, especially when proton PMRT is anticipated.

open_questions: Does proton CC excess persist after matching on reconstruction type?
Which PBS superficial dose parameters drive capsular contracture?
Does prepectoral or autologous reconstruction change proton vs photon risk?

studies.name: NRG/RTOG 9804 + E5194 combined analysis (tamoxifen after lumpectomy, DCIS)
studies.tldr: 15-yr IBR 11.4% vs 19.0% with vs without tamoxifen in good-risk DCIS treated by lumpectomy without RT; invasive IBR HR 0.43.
details: 🔍 Exploratory pooled analysis: non-RT arm of NRG/RTOG 9804 (n=317) + E5194 good-risk cohort (n=561)
🔍 Good-risk: low/intermediate grade DCIS, ≤2.5 cm, excision margins ≥3 mm, no RT
💊 Tamoxifen optional in both trials: 43.1% overall, 65.6% RTOG 9804 vs 30.3% E5194
🔍 Median f/u 14.85 yr (13.87 RTOG 9804, 16.15 E5194); Fine-Gray models

details.text: 📊 IBR outcomes by tamoxifen use (117 IBRs: 65 invasive, 52 DCIS)
⚠️ Baseline imbalance: tamoxifen users skewed lower-risk

details: ⚠️ Multivariable covariates not listed in source; trial membership co-varies with tamoxifen use
⚠️ Tamoxifen dose, duration, adherence not reported in source
⚠️ CBE and OS were estimated but results not in source text
🔗 RTOG 9804 RT arm not analyzed; no tamoxifen-alone vs RT comparison here

verdict.rationale: Exploratory ancillary analysis; tamoxifen optional, not randomized, and imbalanced by trial, re-excision and size. Parent RCT tested RT, not tamoxifen, so residual confounding limits causal read.
verdict.audience: Good-risk DCIS, lumpectomy without RT, low/int grade, ≤2.5 cm, margins ≥3 mm

studies.significance: The association was confined to invasive events (DCIS-IBR p=0.089), which made up 65 of 117 IBRs. For the RT-omission discussion, the 11.4% 15-yr IBR on tamoxifen has no RT arm in this analysis to benchmark against, and which good-risk subgroups drive it sits in Fig 3, with subgroup HRs not in source text.
studies.monday_clinic: In low/intermediate-grade DCIS ≤2.5 cm with margins ≥3 mm managed without RT after lumpectomy, this supports tamoxifen as an invasive-IBR risk-reduction option in the omission discussion; it does not extend to high-grade DCIS or pts receiving RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Ancillary exploratory analysis** combining the non-RT arm of NRG/RTOG 9804, which randomized good-risk DCIS to RT or no RT, with the good-risk E5194 cohort observed without RT. **Tamoxifen was optional and not randomized** in either trial. Univariate and multivariable **Fine-Gray** models; median follow-up **14.85 yr**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **N=878** (317 RTOG 9804, 561 E5194); median age 59 (28-88). Good-risk: **low- or intermediate-grade, ≤2.5 cm, excision margins ≥3 mm**, lumpectomy without RT.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Tamoxifen, optional per trial; used by **43.1%** overall (65.6% RTOG 9804 vs 30.3% E5194). Dose, duration and adherence not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **No RT** in the analyzed population. The RTOG 9804 RT arm is not part of this analysis, so tamoxifen alone is **not compared against RT** here.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **IBR** (any), invasive IBR, DCIS-IBR, contralateral breast event and overall survival. CBE and OS results are not reported in the source text.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 117 IBRs (65 invasive, 52 DCIS). The reduction tracked **invasive IBR, not DCIS-IBR**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: NSABP B-24 randomized tamoxifen after lumpectomy plus RT, and the UK/ANZ DCIS trial randomized tamoxifen and RT in a factorial design. Here tamoxifen is examined **only in good-risk pts managed without RT**, and without randomization.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents low- or intermediate-grade DCIS ≤2.5 cm with margins ≥3 mm treated with lumpectomy without RT. Does not represent high-grade DCIS or pts who received RT after lumpectomy.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Multivariable covariates are not listed in source, and trial membership also differs in follow-up (13.87 vs 16.15 yr). The **DCIS-IBR result (p=0.089) rests on 52 events** and does not exclude an effect.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Tamoxifen use tracked **lower invasive recurrence** in good-risk DCIS managed without RT, consistent in direction with randomized tamoxifen data. It does not settle whether tamoxifen alone approaches RT, or how much of the gap reflects the lower-risk profile of users.

studies.interpretation:
RTOG 9804 and E5194 are the two datasets that made RT omission a defensible conversation in good-risk DCIS: one randomized RT against observation, the other followed a comparable cohort without RT. Neither was built to ask what tamoxifen contributes once RT is dropped, because both left endocrine therapy to choice. This combined analysis turns that choice into an exposure, across 878 pts with a median follow-up of 14.85 years, and finds lower ipsilateral recurrence among users, with 15-year IBR of 11.4% versus 19.0% and an adjusted invasive IBR HR of 0.43.

Against the randomized tamoxifen evidence the direction is unsurprising. NSABP B-24 tested tamoxifen after lumpectomy plus RT, and the UK/ANZ DCIS trial examined tamoxifen and RT together in a factorial design. What this dataset adds is population and horizon rather than a new mechanism: a defined good-risk group (low or intermediate grade, size up to 2.5 cm, margins of at least 3 mm) managed without RT, followed long enough to capture late ipsilateral events. Agreement in direction with randomized data raises plausibility. It does not convert an observational contrast into a randomized estimate for this population.

The confidence a reader places in the magnitude should be tempered by who took the drug. Users were more often RTOG 9804 enrollees (55.0% vs 21.8%), more often had pathologic size ≤5 mm (57.0% vs 41.3%) and more often had a negative re-excision (27.2% vs 10.6%). Each of those plausibly lowers recurrence on its own. The Fine-Gray models adjust, but the source text does not list the covariates, and trial membership bundles differences a single term may not absorb, including follow-up length (13.87 years in RTOG 9804, 16.15 in E5194). Exposure is also coarse: dose, duration and adherence are not reported. Direction is more credible than size, and if residual confounding runs the expected way, the adjusted HRs sit on the favorable side of the true effect.

The split between recurrence types deserves attention. The association held for invasive IBR (p=0.0048) but not DCIS-IBR (p=0.089), with 65 and 52 events respectively. A non-significant result on 52 events is weak evidence of no effect, so the honest reading is that the analysis could not show a DCIS-IBR reduction, not that tamoxifen spares only invasive disease. If the invasive-only pattern is real, it is the more consequential direction for an omission discussion.

For a radiation oncologist, the decision this informs is how to frame RT omission. It quantifies what pts choosing tamoxifen without RT still carry, an 11.4% 15-year IBR estimate, but the analysis includes no RT arm, so it cannot say whether tamoxifen alone approaches RT or whether combining them would add further control. It also does not reach high-grade DCIS. The finding would be wrong in its magnitude if the lower-risk profile of users, not the drug, explains most of the gap; the subgroup forest plot (Fig 3, HRs not in source text) and the unreported contralateral and survival results are where that would show.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For RT omission in good-risk DCIS, tamoxifen alone still left 15-yr IBR at 11.4%, and this analysis has no RT arm to benchmark it against. The reduction tracked invasive IBR (HR 0.43), while DCIS-IBR did not separate (p=0.089).
significance_by_specialty.medonc: In good-risk DCIS managed without RT, tamoxifen associated with lower invasive IBR (HR 0.43, 0.24-0.77) but not DCIS-IBR (p=0.089). Dose, duration and adherence are not reported, and contralateral breast event results, the other half of the endocrine rationale, are not in source text.

open_questions: Does tamoxifen alone approximate RT for IBR control in good-risk DCIS?
Which good-risk DCIS subgroups gain enough to justify tamoxifen?
Is the lack of DCIS-IBR reduction real or underpowered?

sites.intro: Unlike QD escalation in CONVERT and CALGB 30610/RTOG 0538, involved-field BID SIB escalation to 54 Gy improved OS; the 39.5 mo control arm beats prior 45 Gy BID arms, so transfer depends on selection (PET-staged, ECOG 0–1, age ≤70).

studies.name: High-dose hyperfractionated SIB RT vs standard-dose RT for limited-stage SCLC
studies.tldr: mOS 60.7 vs 39.5 mo, HR 0.55 (0.37–0.72), p=0.003 with 54 Gy/30 fx BID SIB vs 45 Gy/30 fx BID in LS-SCLC; toxicity similar.
details: 🔍 Open-label randomised phase 3, 16 hospitals in China, N=224 (108 vs 116), median f/u 46 mo
🔍 54 Gy/30 fx SIB to GTV/IGTV (PTV 45 Gy) vs 45 Gy/30 fx, both BID VMAT over 3 wks
🔍 Involved field only: PET-CT-positive primary + nodes, no elective nodal irradiation
💊 Concurrent cisplatin or carboplatin + etoposide × 4, TRT started 0–42 days after cycle 1
⚠️ DSMB stopped at interim (88 deaths, 224 of 326 planned): HR 0.50 (0.32–0.78), p=0.002
⚠️ Control mOS 39.5 mo exceeds prior 45 Gy BID arms (20.8–30 mo): age 18–70, ECOG 0–1, PET-staged

details.text: 🔗 Dose escalation vs 45 Gy BID across randomised trials, as cited in source

verdict.rationale: Stopped at interim for benefit with 224 of 326 planned accrued; truncated RCTs tend to overstate effect. Single-country, open-label, no central RT QA, age ≤70.
verdict.audience: LS-SCLC (VALSG), age 18–70, ECOG 0–1, PET-CT and brain MRI staged

studies.significance: Escalation is a GTV/IGTV-only SIB (PTV held at 45 Gy) within the same 30 fx, 3-week BID course on PET-defined involved fields. Local PFS separated (HR 0.51) while MFS did not (HR 0.81), fitting an in-field effect. The decision it moves is BID dose, 45 vs 54 Gy, not BID vs once daily.
studies.monday_clinic: In PET-CT and brain-MRI staged LS-SCLC, age 18–70 and ECOG 0–1, planned for concurrent platinum-etoposide with BID thoracic RT, this supports 54 Gy SIB as an alternative to 45 Gy; it does not extend to pts over 70, ECOG 2, or once-daily schedules.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Open-label randomised phase 3**, 1:1, 16 public hospitals in China, N=224 (108 vs 116) enrolled June 2017 to April 2021. Stratified by ECOG, stage, prior chemo courses and platinum choice. **Stopped early by the DSMB** at the interim after 88 deaths; median follow-up 46 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Age 18–70, ECOG 0–1**, LS-SCLC by VALSG staging, with mandatory whole-body **PET-CT and brain MRI**. Untreated or after 1–2 courses of platinum-etoposide. Median age 64; 86% stage III; 79% current or former smokers.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Cisplatin 75 mg/m² or carboplatin AUC 5 plus etoposide 100 mg/m² days 1–3, 4 courses every 3 weeks; almost 99% received all 4. PCI 25 Gy/10 fx for responders (82% vs 81%).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **54 Gy/30 fx SIB to GTV/IGTV with PTV at 45 Gy** vs 45 Gy/30 fx, both VMAT, BID at least 6 h apart, 5 days/wk for 3 weeks, starting 0–42 days after chemo cycle 1. Involved field: PET-positive primary and nodes, CTV = GTV + 5 mm, **no elective nodal irradiation**. Constraints included MLD ≤15 Gy, lung V20 <30%, cord max ≤40 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** OS in ITT, measured from chemo start. **Secondary:** PFS, local PFS, MFS, DCR, acute and late toxicity (CTCAE v5.0), HRQOL (to be reported separately). Powered on HR 0.65 at 81% power, target 326 pts.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary endpoint crossed the interim boundary and held at the January 2023 cutoff, with 40 (37%) vs 66 (57%) deaths. Arm-level estimates are in the efficacy table.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute G3–4 RT toxicity similar between arms. No late G3 oesophagitis or stricture in either arm; late G3 pneumonitis in 2 vs 3 pts, no G3 pulmonary fibrosis. **One treatment-related death** (myocardial infarction) in the 54 Gy arm.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: INT-0096 set 45 Gy/30 fx BID as the reference. **CONVERT** (66 Gy/33 fx QD) and **CALGB 30610/RTOG 0538** (70 Gy QD) escalated dose without acceleration or hyperfractionation and did not beat it; the Northern European randomised phase 2 of 60 Gy/40 fx BID was the only prior BID escalation signal. The authors describe this as the first phase 3 to escalate while keeping BID delivery.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents fit, PET-CT and brain-MRI staged LS-SCLC pts aged 18–70 with ECOG 0–1 receiving concurrent platinum-etoposide. Does not represent pts over 70, ECOG 2, or anyone staged without PET-CT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Control mOS of 39.5 mo beat the 24 mo design assumption and prior 45 Gy BID arms (20.8–30 mo), marking a selected cohort. Tumour and RT volumes were not controlled, and the interim analysis is listed as the only protocol amendment despite being described as preplanned. Reporting inconsistencies: median age given as both 64 and 62, and the OS CI upper bound (62.0) sits just above the 60.7 mo median.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The authors credit **local control** for the OS gain, but first-relapse rates were near identical (59 [55%] vs 65 [56%]) and chest-first failure **did not differ significantly**, so patterns of failure do not yet show where the benefit arises. Subgroup and HRQOL results are unreported.

studies.interpretation:
For a radiation oncologist who already treats limited-stage disease twice daily, the escalation question has mostly been tested sideways. INT-0096 made 45 Gy in 30 BID fractions the reference, and the two phase 3 attempts to improve on it, CONVERT at 66 Gy in 33 once-daily fractions and CALGB 30610/RTOG 0538 at 70 Gy once daily, raised dose while giving up acceleration and hyperfractionation. Neither improved survival, which left unresolved whether dose was the wrong lever or whether abandoning the short BID course cancelled any gain. This trial isolates the variable: same 30 fractions, same three weeks, same 45 Gy PTV, with only the GTV/IGTV boosted to 54 Gy. The Northern European randomised phase 2 of 60 Gy in 40 BID fractions pointed the same way, so the direction is now supported by two randomised datasets.

The magnitude deserves less trust than the direction. The DSMB stopped the trial after 88 deaths with 224 of 326 planned pts accrued, when the interim HR was 0.50; with follow-up to January 2023 it sat at 0.55. Trials truncated for benefit tend to overstate effect, and drift toward the null as events accrue is the expected pattern. An upper CI bound of 0.72 leaves room for a real benefit even if the estimate shrinks further, but the 21.2-month median gain the authors cite should not be carried to tumor board as a stable figure.

The control arm is the second caution. Standard-dose pts reached a median OS of 39.5 mo, against 20.8–30 mo in earlier 45 Gy BID cohorts and a 24-month design assumption. The authors point to VALSG staging, mandatory PET-CT and brain MRI, and exclusion of ECOG 2 and anyone over 70, in a disease whose NCDB median age is 67. Selection does not bias the randomised contrast, but absolute medians will not transfer, and the relative benefit is untested in the older, less fit pts seen in practice. Open-label assessment matters little for OS but more for investigator-read PFS and local PFS, and with no central RT quality assurance across 16 centres, contour and delivered-dose consistency are unverified.

The mechanism is plausible but not closed. Local PFS favoured 54 Gy (HR 0.51) while MFS did not separate (HR 0.81, p=0.248), which fits an in-field effect. Yet first-relapse rates were 55% vs 56% and chest-first failure did not differ significantly, so the local-control story is not visible in first-site failure data, which record where relapse began rather than later in-field progression. Toxicity parity is the other half of the case: G3–4 acute oesophagitis 13% vs 12%, against the 32% the authors cite from INT-0096, delivered with VMAT, 4D-CT, cone-beam verification and involved fields. That parity likely depends on a GTV-only boost within PET-restricted volumes and may not hold with elective nodal fields or larger boost volumes.

What it moves: for a fit, PET-staged pt already planned for concurrent chemo with BID thoracic RT, a 54 Gy SIB is a defensible alternative to 45 Gy. What it leaves open: whether 54 Gy in 30 fractions matches or beats 60 Gy in 40 BID fractions, whether benefit survives beyond age 70, and how a higher GTV dose behaves alongside consolidation immunotherapy, which was not part of this chemo-only protocol.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: A GTV/IGTV-only boost to 54 Gy with PTV at 45 Gy keeps 30 fx BID over 3 weeks on involved PET-defined fields, with G3–4 acute oesophagitis 13% vs 12%. The actionable choice is BID dose, 45 vs 54 Gy, for fit PET-staged pts; once-daily escalation is not addressed.

open_questions: Does the 54 Gy SIB benefit hold in pts older than 70 or ECOG 2?
54 Gy/30 fx SIB BID vs 60 Gy/40 fx BID or high-dose once-daily?
Does higher thoracic dose add benefit alongside consolidation immunotherapy?

papers.title: Impact of Tamoxifen Only After Lumpectomy for "Good-Risk" Duct Carcinoma In Situ: Combined Analysis of the NRG Oncology/RTOG 9804 and ECOG-ACRIN E5194 Trials.
papers.journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: The NRG Oncology/Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) 9804 trial randomized patients with "good-risk" ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) to radiation (RT) or no RT following lumpectomy. The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group-American College of Radiology Imaging Network E5194 trial had a comparable cohort observed without RT. Tamoxifen use was optional in both trials. This ancillary exploratory analysis combining both data sets assessed the effect of tamoxifen on ipsilateral breast recurrence (IBR) in "good-risk" DCIS treated with lumpectomy alone.

METHODS AND MATERIALS: A combined database from the non-RT arm of NRG/RTOG 9804 and the "good-risk" cohort from E5194 (low- or intermediate-grade, ≤2.5 cm, excision margins ≥3 mm) was created, and distributions of patient and DCIS characteristics by tamoxifen use were compared by χ2. IBR, invasive IBR, DCIS-IBR, contralateral breast event, and overall survival were estimated, and distributions were compared between tamoxifen use groups. Univariate and multivariable Fine-Gray regression models were used to analyze factors that may be associated with endpoints.

RESULTS: Eight hundred and seventy-eight patients were analyzed (317 from NRG/RTOG 9804 and 561 from E5194). The use of tamoxifen overall was 43.1% (65.6% in NRG/RTOG 9804 and 30.3% in E5194). At a median follow-up of 14.85 years, there were 117 IBRs (65 invasive and 52 DCIS). There was a significant association for reduced IBR with tamoxifen use (P = .001); estimated 15-year IBR with tamoxifen is 11.4% (95% CI, 7.9-15.5) and without is 19.0% (15.3-22.9). Tamoxifen use was significantly associated with reduced invasive IBR (P = .0048) but not DCIS-IBR (P = .089). On multivariable analysis, patients who received tamoxifen were 46% less likely to have any IBR (hazard ratio, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.35-0.83; P = .0045), and 57% less likely to have invasive IBR (hazard ratio, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.24-0.77; P = 0.0042).

CONCLUSION: For patients with "good-risk" DCIS treated with lumpectomy without RT, tamoxifen use was significantly associated with a reduction in IBR overall and invasive IBR, not DCIS-IBR.

papers.title: Does Pencil Beam Scanning Proton Therapy Impart a Higher Risk of Capsular Contracture Compared With Intensity Modulated Photon Radiation Therapy in the Postmastectomy Reconstruction Setting?
papers.journal: International journal of radiation oncology, biology, physics
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Postmastectomy radiation therapy (PMRT) may cause adverse events in the reconstruction setting. Proton-based PMRT is increasingly used and has been shown to improve cardiac and pulmonary dosimetry. Data on the risk of capsular contracture (CC) with proton versus photon PMRT remain scarce. We compared the CC rate of the largest cohort of patients undergoing reconstruction after pencil beam scanning proton PMRT reported to date with an intensity modulated radiation therapy photon cohort, hypothesizing that the proton cohort would have a higher rate of CC.

METHODS AND MATERIALS: An institutional review board -approved retrospective study was conducted on patients with breast cancer who underwent subpectoral 2-stage tissue expander/implant (TE/I) or direct-to-implant (DTI) breast reconstruction and received either pencil beam scanning proton or intensity modulated radiation therapy photon PMRT between January 2017 and December 2023 at 2 centers within a single institution. All patients undergoing TE/I had the TE irradiated. CC rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Cox proportional hazards analysis, denoted as hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs, was used to assess variables potentially associated with the outcome, and a binary logistic regression model was used to verify the results.

RESULTS: The study cohort comprised 175 patients (89 proton; 86 photon). The median age was 49 years (range, 24-78), 63% were Hispanic. Patient demographics were well balanced between the groups, except in tumor laterality (P < .001) and reconstruction type (TE/I vs DTI; P < .001). The median follow-up was 42 and 47 months for the proton and photon groups, respectively. In a multivariable analysis, DTI patients had a significantly higher risk of CC compared with TE/I patients (HR, 3.0; 95% CI, 1.7-5.5; P < .001). Proton patients had a higher risk of developing CC compared with the photon group in univariate analysis (HR, 2.3; 95% CI, 1.26-4.30; P = .007), although this effect did not reach statistical significance in the multivariable model (HR, 1.76; 95% CI, 0.93-3.32; P = .083). The 2-year CC rate for patients treated with protons and DTI (n = 36), photons and DTI (n = 15), protons and TE/I (n = 53), and photons and TE/I (n = 71) was 50%, 35%, 23%, 12%, respectively (P < .001). No other factors were significantly associated with CC development.

CONCLUSION: In this contemporary large proton versus photon PMRT cohort, patients treated with proton showed a trend toward an increased risk of CC. Patients undergoing DTI who were treated with protons had the highest risk of CC (50%). Careful consideration of reconstruction and radiation therapy modalities, assessing CC risk, and also involving patient input, is important for treatment selection.
